podcast.title: Covered "1969"
podcast.body: The Black Keys are among the artists who have covered The Stooges' song "1969." "Tracks on this album have been covered by the Sex Pistols, Joey Ramone, Sonic Youth, the Sisters of Mercy, Joan Jett, Red Cross, and the Black Keys."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Stooges?

podcast.title: Formation and Early Independent Success (2001)
podcast.body: Dan Auerbach and Patrick Carney formed the band in 2001 in Accord, Ohio. They released a series of independent albums that, while generally well-reviewed, received limited attention beyond a dedicated fan base prior to their mainstream breakthrough. "Dan Auerbach and Patrick Carney first got together in 2001 in Accord Ohio, and they released a series of independent albums that were generally well-reviewed, but didn't receive much attention outside of a tight circle of fans."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 00's Part 2: The Indie Revolution

podcast.title: Band Tension and Patrick Carney's Divorce (2010)
podcast.body: During the period surrounding the recording of *Brothers*, significant internal tension arose between Dan Auerbach and Patrick Carney. Patrick acknowledged they were "sick of each other" and maintained separate lives outside of band work. This was compounded by Dan's solo album (made without Patrick's knowledge, which upset him), and Patrick's tumultuous divorce from his wife, Denise. Dan believed Denise was "bad news," and she was accused of cheating, playing mind games, and taking money. Patrick consequently suffered from depression and began drinking, leading the band to the brink of collapse, until he divorced his wife over the phone while the band was in Europe, after which their relationship and the band's dynamic began to improve. "Then there was the drama between Dan and Patrick's wife Denise."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up With The Black Keys

podcast.title: Dan Auerbach's Divorce (2014)
podcast.body: The creation of the *Turn Blue* album was heavily influenced by Dan Auerbach's divorce. A widely circulated anecdote claimed a custody battle over "a lock of Bob Dylan's hair," but this was a misunderstanding; the actual dispute was over a poster of Bob Dylan with large hair, which was colloquially referred to as "Bob Dylan's hair." "And just like brothers, was Patrick Kernie's divorce album, this one was informed by Dan's divorce."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up With The Black Keys

podcast.title: "Grey Ghost" Van
podcast.body: In their early touring days, The Black Keys used a 1994 Chrysler van, which they affectionately named "The Grey Ghost," to travel between gigs. A similar old Chrysler van later featured prominently on the album cover of *El Camino*. "they were just scraping by and chugging from gig to gig in a 1994 Chrysler van that they called the Grey Ghost..."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up With The Black Keys

podcast.title: Accidental Band Formation
podcast.body: The Black Keys formed when Dan Auerbach, seeking to create a demo as a singer-songwriter, asked Patrick Carney, who owned a 4-track recorder, for help. They invited musician friends to round out the sound, but only Dan and Patrick showed up on the scheduled recording day, leading them to form the band as a duo out of necessity. "On the appointed day, no one except Dan and Patrick showed up. So that left the two of them to form a band on their own."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up With The Black Keys

podcast.title: Accidental Band Formation
podcast.body: Dan Auerbach and Patrick Carney, who met around ages 8 or 9 and became friends in high school in Akron, Ohio (both briefly attending the University of Akron), initially planned to record a demo for Dan's solo singer-songwriter pursuits. They invited musician friends to Patrick's basement, but on the appointed day in 2001, only Dan and Patrick appeared, leading them to spontaneously form a duo. "On the appointed day, no one except Dan and Patrick showed up. So that left the two of them to form a band on their own."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up With The Black Keys

podcast.title: Akron, Ohio Roots
podcast.body: Both Dan Auerbach and Patrick Carney hail from Akron, Ohio, having met around ages 8 or 9. They became friends in high school, despite contrasting personalities (Dan as a "jock" and Patrick as a "nerd"), and both attended the University of Akron. Their hometown's historical significance as a tire manufacturing hub and their attendance at Firestone High School are notable local connections. "Dan and Patrick are both from Akron, Ohio."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up With The Black Keys

podcast.title: Album Announcement by Mike Tyson
podcast.body: The Black Keys' *Turn Blue* album was uniquely announced by boxer Mike Tyson via a tweet, creating an unusual media buzz around its release. "Its existence was announced by Mike Tyson, yes, him in a tweet."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up With The Black Keys

podcast.title: Album Announcement by Mike Tyson
podcast.body: The release of The Black Keys' *Turn Blue* album was publicly announced through a tweet by boxer Mike Tyson. "Its existence was announced by Mike Tyson, yes, him, in a tweet."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up With The Black Keys

podcast.title: Altercation Between Patrick Carney and Jack White
podcast.body: On September 13, 2015, Patrick Carney of The Black Keys encountered Jack White at a New York City bar called Cabin Down Below. Carney, who had never met White before, claimed White attempted to fight him, describing White as a "40-year-old bully." White denied any physical fight, stating he merely asked a question Carney couldn't answer. "Patrick, I've never met Jack White until last night. He came to a bar in New York City, I go to a lot with a few friends and tried to fight me."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Modern Rock Feuds

podcast.title: Band Internal Crisis (Brothers Era)
podcast.body: During the period leading up to and during the *Brothers* album, Dan Auerbach and Patrick Carney faced severe interpersonal conflicts, with Patrick explicitly stating they were not "friends" outside of band work. Tensions escalated when Dan recorded a solo album without Patrick's knowledge, leading to months of silence, and further complicated by drama involving Patrick's wife, Denise, whom Dan disliked. Denise's alleged infidelity, "mind games," and financial misconduct contributed to Patrick's depression and increased drinking, bringing the band close to collapse until Patrick ended his marriage while on tour in Europe, which helped restore the band's stability. "The thing that probably kept the block keys together at this point was some stuff that initially kept them apart."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up With The Black Keys

podcast.title: Breakthrough Delay
podcast.body: It took The Black Keys until the release of their sixth album to achieve their significant breakthrough into wider recognition. "It took them until album number six for them to have their big breakthrough."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up With Twenty One Pilots

podcast.title: Comparison to The White Stripes
podcast.body: The Black Keys' career benefited from the concurrent rise of The White Stripes, another prominent "garaji, punky, two-piece band." As The White Stripes gained mainstream attention, public interest in The Black Keys also grew, indicating a shared musical space and audience appreciation for their raw sound. "The bigger the white stripes got, the more interesting to grow in the black keys."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up With The Black Keys

podcast.title: Comparison to The White Stripes
podcast.body: The Black Keys experienced an increase in interest and profile due to the rising popularity of The White Stripes, another garage-punk two-piece band. The greater success achieved by The White Stripes inadvertently helped to draw more attention to The Black Keys. "The bigger the white stripes got, the more interesting to grow in the black keys."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up With The Black Keys

podcast.title: Contemporaries in the Mid-2000s
podcast.body: During their early and mid-2000s period, The Black Keys shared the scene with other notable indie bands such as Vampire Weekend, The National, Interpol, The Hold Steady, and Gaslight Anthem. "Their contemporaries at the time included Vampire Weekend, We Had The National, Interpol, The Hold Steady, and Gas Line Anthem."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 00's Part 2: The Indie Revolution

podcast.title: Continued Activity in 2010s
podcast.body: This established band continued its characteristic musical output throughout the 2010s, contrasting with the softer pop alt-rock trend. "Older groups, the food fighters, Lincoln Park, Black Keys, Chili Peppers, Green Day, Queens of the Stone Age, Royal Blood, Muse, Blink 182, Pearl Jam, they just kept doing what they did best."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 2: The Role of Indie Rock

podcast.title: DIY Recording Environment
podcast.body: The band recorded their album "Rubber Factory" in an abandoned tire warehouse they rented for $500 a month, utilizing only used gear and recycled recording tape, demonstrating a strong DIY ethic. "They were working out of an abandoned tire warehouse that they rated for $500 a month, and they were recording on used gear using recycled recording tape."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 00's Part 2: The Indie Revolution

podcast.title: Dan Auerbach Banned from Third Man Studios
podcast.body: As part of the ongoing feud, Dan Auerbach was explicitly banned from Jack White's Third Man Studios in Nashville. "Hourback was banned from ever-setting foot in Jack's third-man studios in Nashville."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Dan Auerbach's Divorce Album (Turn Blue)
podcast.body: The *Turn Blue* album is characterized as Dan Auerbach's divorce album, with its lyrics providing insights into his "weird divorce" experiences. A notable anecdote involved a public misunderstanding that he was battling over a lock of Bob Dylan's hair, when in fact, the dispute centered on a poster featuring Bob Dylan with "really big hair," which they informally referred to as "Bob Dylan's hair." "Turn blue, the eighth album, was recorded in fits and starts over more than a year and a half before being released on May 12, 2014."

podcast.title: Dan Auerbach's Solo Career
podcast.body: In 2009, Dan Auerbach released a solo album titled *Keep It Hid*. He is also an in-demand producer, with notable credits including records for Dr. John and Hacienda. "Dan Orrback has that 2009 solo album entitled Keep It Head."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up With The Black Keys

podcast.title: Early Demo (Holy Grail)
podcast.body: The Black Keys' very first demo, recorded by Dan Auerbach and Patrick Carney with Gary Fumovar on keyboards, was submitted to numerous indie labels, but only Alive Records showed interest. This demo is now considered a "holy grail" by hardcore fans, though Dan and Patrick themselves deem it "very substandard" and prefer it not to be heard. "That demo, the one they sent out to all these indie labels, is like the holy grail to hardcore block keys fans."

podcast.title: Early Withdrawal from Woodstock 50
podcast.body: The Black Keys were among the first artists to withdraw from the planned Woodstock 50 festival in 2019 once the numerous logistical problems and general chaos surrounding the event became obvious. Their decision reflected growing concerns among performers about the festival's safety and viability, particularly in light of the disastrous Woodstock 99. "One of the first bands to bail when it became obvious that there would be trouble was these guys, The Black Keys."

podcast.title: Embracing Cheap Instruments
podcast.body: The Black Keys are listed among indie revival bands that adopted inexpensive instruments to project an anti-establishment image. This choice served as a statement against the perceived elitism of vintage or high-end guitar culture. "They wouldn't be caught dead playing, let’s say a vintage-less paw, think white stripes, yeah, yeah, yeah, and the strokes and the black keys."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Story of the Electric Guitar - Part 3

podcast.title: Evolution of Licensing Stance
podcast.body: The band later revised their stance on song licensing, allowing their music to be used in various commercial contexts, including movies, TV shows (Sony), video games, and advertisements for products like jeans, Nissan, American Express, and Victoria's Secret. This shift reflected a growing priority for financial stability and sustaining their career on the road over strictly adhering to an "anti-sell-out" position. "These opportunities came along when Pagan the Ranton's Day on the Road was more important than preserving some kind of anti-sale-out stance."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up With The Black Keys

podcast.title: Extensive Discography
podcast.body: The Black Keys' extensive catalog, often underestimated by casual listeners, includes 8 full studio albums, 2 EPs, 1 live album, and nearly two dozen singles, alongside various collaborations and tribute recordings. "No, they have 8 full albums, 2 EPs, 1 live album and close to 2 dozen singles."

podcast.title: Feud with Jack White
podcast.body: Jack White harbored disdain for The Black Keys, particularly guitarist Dan Auerbach, whom he called a "copycat." The animosity escalated when White accused Auerbach of interfering in his custody dispute with ex-wife Karen Elson, specifically over their children attending the same Nashville private school as Auerbach's children from another relationship. Leaked emails from 2013 contained "vicious" remarks. "For some reason, Jack had a disdain for guitarist Dan Hourback, calling him a copycat and calling him out for allegedly getting involved in the custody battle he was having with Karen Elson, that ex-wife."

podcast.title: Grammy Awards - The Black Keys Accolades
podcast.body: The Black Keys received five Grammy nominations for *Brothers*, winning Best Alternative Album and Best Artwork. For *El Camino*, they won Best Rock Album and two awards for "Lonely Boy," with Dan Auerbach also earning Producer of the Year. "The Brothers record was big too, with five Grammy nominations overall. It won for Best Alternative Album, and it picked up an award for Best Artwork."

podcast.title: Gullardi Influence on Album Title and Art
podcast.body: The title *Turn Blue* was inspired by a catchphrase of Gullardi, a Cleveland late-night horror movie show host from the 1960s, serving as an homage. The album's cover art also reflects Gullardi's interest in films centered on themes of mind control, brainwashing, and hypnotism. "The title was co-opted from a catchphrase by a dude named Gullardy, who hosted a late night horror movie show in Cleveland back in the 1960s."

podcast.title: Jack White's Conditional Apology
podcast.body: In spring 2014, Jack White issued a public apology on his website, wishing The Black Keys "all the success that they can get" and acknowledging the challenges faced by two-piece bands. "I wish the Black Keys all the success that they can get, he said. Lord knows that I can tell you myself how hard it is to get people to pay attention to a two-piece band with a plastic guitar."

podcast.title: Japanese Album Title Change
podcast.body: The Black Keys' album *Thickfreakness* was retitled *Inezuma Rock and Blues* for its Japanese release because the original title did not translate well, with "Inezuma" meaning lightning in Japanese. "So that's why they decided to call it Inezuma Rock and Blues. Inezuma means lightning in Japanese."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up With The Black Keys

podcast.title: Junior Kimbrough's Influence on Dan Auerbach
podcast.body: Junior Kimbrough, a blues singer and the subject of The Black Keys' *Chulahoma* EP, was a profound influence on Dan Auerbach. Dan was a devoted fan in high school, and listening to Kimbrough, particularly while smoking marijuana, proved to be a pivotal experience that guided his decision to pursue a full-time career as a guitarist. "In fact, listening to Kimbrough, while smoking a lot of dope, helped him decide to pursue the guitar full time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up With The Black Keys

podcast.title: Later Revival Artist & Ohio Home
podcast.body: The Black Keys are noted as a later band in the Garage Rock revival. Their home city of Akron, Ohio, is also highlighted as the original home of Chrissie Hynde and The Pretenders, and a regional influence for Karen O. of the Ye-Eyes. "And just an hour away was Akron, the original home of Christy Hine and the pretenders, and the home of the Black Keys."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Revivals Part 4: Garage Rock

podcast.title: Later Song Licensing
podcast.body: After an initial refusal of a significant commercial licensing deal, the band later reversed its stance, licensing many of its songs for use in movies, TV shows, video games, and products from companies such as Sony, Nissan, American Express, and Victoria's Secret. This change of heart occurred when financial needs, such as paying rent and sustaining touring, became more pressing than maintaining an anti-sell-out image. "Later, they'd have a change of heart, and plenty of black keys songs would be licensed for movies and TV and products by Sony, video games, jeans, Nissan, American Express, and even Victoria's Secret."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up With The Black Keys

podcast.title: Mayonnaise Commercial Offer
podcast.body: Early in their career, a UK-based mayonnaise manufacturer offered The Black Keys 200,000 pounds for the use of one of their songs in a TV commercial. Despite struggling financially and touring in their 1994 Chrysler van known as "The Grey Ghost," the band declined the offer, believing it would harm their artistic integrity, a decision that infuriated their parents. "The manufacturer of a brand of mayonnaise based on the UK offered the keys 200,000 pounds for the use of one of their songs."

podcast.title: Partial Resistance to Spotify
podcast.body: The Black Keys, considered an "indie" group, were initially strong opponents of Spotify. While shared rights prevented them from removing their entire discography, they refused to publish the portion they fully controlled. Eventually, they yielded to the platform. "Los Blackis o placebo que también han sido grandes enemigos. Spotify que no podían quitar toda su discografía por temas de derechos compartidos, pero la parte en la que tenían total control de su discografía, así se negaban a publicarla, que también al final se acababan rindiendo de la como, ¡Mira, tomadla porque esto no puede enfrentarme a ti!"

podcast.title: Patrick Carney's Divorce Album (Brothers)
podcast.body: The *Brothers* album is retrospectively linked to Patrick Carney's tumultuous marriage and subsequent divorce, reflecting his personal struggles during its creation. "I talked to both of them around this time, and I came away with a distinct impression that these guys were a bit sick of each other."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up With The Black Keys

podcast.title: Patrick Carney's Side Projects and Production
podcast.body: Patrick Carney operates his own indie label, Audio Eagle Records, which signed the band Drummer. He also joined Drummer in the studio, playing bass, despite the band's members all being drummers from other groups. Carney's production work includes contributing to The Sheepdogs' 2012 debut record, as well as albums for Tennis and Tobias Gesso Jr. "Patrick Carney was watching an indie band called Drummer, who was signed to his audio-eagle records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up With The Black Keys

podcast.title: Prominent Two-Piece Band
podcast.body: The Black Keys are cited as one of the two-piece bands that emerged in the early 2000s, marking the increasing prevalence of this format in rock music. "But we also saw the appearance of 21 pilots, the block keys, dressed in dolls, the kills, the Khalifa mods, the Ravianettes, and the load more."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 6: (50-41)

podcast.title: Record Album CD Color Change
podcast.body: The physical CD for The Black Keys' *Brothers* album was designed with a unique feature: it would change color (black to white in the US, white to black in Australia, silver to black in Europe) when heated by a CD player's laser during playback. "See, out of the package, the CD is black. But as it heats up with the laser in your CD player as it plays, it turns white."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up With The Black Keys

podcast.title: Recording Studio in Tire Factory
podcast.body: For their third album, *Rubber Factory*, The Black Keys repurposed the second floor of a former General Tire factory in East Akron, Ohio, renting the space for $500 a month. This unique studio choice highlighted their connection to their hometown's industrial heritage, as Akron was a major tire manufacturing hub, and they even attended Firestone High School. "The third album was recorded in a different spot, and the band-in-tire factory in East Akron that was once run by General Tyre".

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up With The Black Keys

podcast.title: Recording in Abandoned Studio
podcast.body: The Black Keys specifically chose to record ten tracks for their "Brothers" album in the long-abandoned Muscle Shoals Sound Studio, bringing all their own equipment and enduring dusty conditions, driven by a profound desire to absorb the studio's historical "vibes." "They wanted to record their sixth album at Muscle Shoals. They had to do it in that studio, even though the place hadn't been used to make records for years."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: More Famous Recording Studios

podcast.title: Rejection of Mayonnaise Commercial Deal
podcast.body: Early in their career, The Black Keys famously turned down a 200,000-pound offer from a UK mayonnaise brand to license one of their songs for a TV commercial. Despite their financial struggles, touring in a 1994 Chrysler van called the "Grey Ghost," they believed accepting the offer would compromise their artistic integrity and "anti-sell-out" image, a decision that angered their parents. "they turned it down because they figured that would damage the credit."

podcast.body: Following a public Twitter exchange, Patrick Carney announced that he had spoken with Jack White for an hour, finding him "cool, all good." Jack White then publicly responded to Carney, saying, "From one musician to another. You have my respect, Patrick Carney," indicating a resolution to their conflict. "Talk to Jack for an hour. podcast.body: The Black Keys contributed to the various *Twilight* soundtracks that accompanied the film series. These soundtracks featured a nice selection of tunes, mostly album cuts and outtakes, from a range of artists spanning different genres. "The Paramore, Lincoln Park, Collective Soul, Death Cab for Cutie, Tom York, the Killers, Editors, Metric, Block Keys, Dead Weather, Beck, Vampire Weekend, Florence in the Machine."

xref.title: "Lonely Boy" Music Video Star
xref.body: Derek T. Tuggle, originally a security guard, achieved unexpected fame as the star of The Black Keys' "Lonely Boy" music video. After an initial video shoot with many extras proved ineffective, Dan Auerbach and Patrick Carney noticed Tuggle's distinctive dancing in preview edits and decided to feature him exclusively in a single-shot video, which quickly amassed nearly half a million YouTube views. "It's a single shot of Derek T. Tuggle dancing to the song."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: "Turn Blue" Album Announcement
xref.body: The release of The Black Keys' *Turn Blue* album was notably announced by boxer Mike Tyson via a tweet, adding an unconventional and high-profile element to its promotion. "Its existence was announced by Mike Tyson, yes, him in a tweet."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up With The Black Keys

xref.title: "Turn Blue" Album Homage
xref.body: Gullardy, a Cleveland host of a late-night horror movie show in the 1960s, is honored in The Black Keys' *Turn Blue* album. The album's title was inspired by his catchphrase, and its cover art visually references his fascination with mind control, brainwashing, and hypnotism as themes in movies. "The title was co-opted from a catchphrase by a dude named Gullardy, who hosted a late night horror movie show in Cleveland back in the 1960s."

"And just an hour away was Akron, the original home of Christy Hine and the pretenders, and the home of the Black Keys."

xref.title: Altercation with Patrick Carney of The Black Keys
xref.body: On September 13, 2015, Jack White ran into Patrick Carney of The Black Keys at a New York City bar called Cabin Down Below. Carney, who had never met White in person, claimed White tried to fight him, calling White a "40-year-old bully" and saying he inspired Carney to play music as a reaction against such "A-holes." White responded on Twitter, denying any physical altercation, stating he merely asked a question that Carney couldn't answer, and urged him to "speak face to face like a human being." "Patrick, I've never met Jack White until last night. He came to a bar in New York City, I go to a lot with a few friends and tried to fight me."

xref.title: Ban from Third Man Studios
xref.body: As part of his feud with The Black Keys, Jack White banned Dan Auerbach from ever setting foot in his Third Man Studios in Nashville. "Hourback was banned from ever-setting foot in Jack's third-man studios in Nashville."

xref.title: Conditional Apology to The Black Keys
xref.body: In the spring of 2014, an apology appeared on Jack White's website, stating, "I wish the Black Keys all the success that they can get." He acknowledged the difficulty of gaining attention for a two-piece band, implying a conditional truce. "I wish the Black Keys all the success that they can get, he said. Lord knows that I can tell you myself how hard it is to get people to pay attention to a two-piece band with a plastic guitar."

xref.title: Early 4-track Recorder Owner
xref.body: Patrick Carney's ownership of a 4-track recorder played a crucial role in the initial stages of The Black Keys' formation. It enabled him and Dan Auerbach to record their first demo, which was essential for Auerbach's aspirations as a singer-songwriter. "Since Patrick had a 4 track recorder, he asked Patrick if he would help him make one of these demos."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Early Ambition as Singer-Songwriter
xref.body: Prior to the formation of The Black Keys, Dan Auerbach aspired to be a singer-songwriter performing in local bars. His need for a demo tape to secure out-of-town gigs led him to seek Patrick Carney's help, which inadvertently initiated their collaboration. "We had this idea of being a singer-songwriter who played the bars in the area, but the no one would give him any out of town gigs without a demo."

xref.title: Early Keyboards Member
xref.body: Gary Fumovar, a friend of Dan Auerbach's younger brother, was an early participant in The Black Keys, contributing keyboards to their foundational demo record. "And there were three keys on this record, by the way. There was Dan, there was Patrick, and Gary Fumovar, a friend of Dan's younger brother who was also there to play keyboards."

xref.title: Embracing Cheap Instruments
xref.body: Jack White is noted for using inexpensive instruments as a deliberate part of his anti-establishment artistic image. This approach contrasts with the use of vintage, high-end guitars and connects him to the indie revival trend of using accessible gear. "They wouldn't be caught dead playing, let's say a vintage-less paw, think white stripes, yeah, yeah, yeah, and the strokes and the black keys."

xref.title: Feud with The Black Keys
xref.body: Jack White expressed disdain for The Black Keys' guitarist Dan Auerbach, calling him a "copycat." The feud intensified when White accused Auerbach of allegedly involving himself in White's custody battle with ex-wife Karen Elson, specifically noting that Auerbach sent his children to the same Nashville private school as White's and Elson's children. Leaked emails from 2013 between White and Elson revealed vicious comments. "For some reason, Jack had a disdain for guitarist Dan Hourback, calling him a copycat and calling him out for allegedly getting involved in the custody battle he was having with Karen Elson, that ex-wife."

xref.body: Danger Mouse's prior commitment to producing an album for Ike Turner initially prevented him from working with The Black Keys on *Attack and Release*. However, the eventual collapse of the Ike Turner project freed him up to collaborate with the band. "Unfortunately, he was unavailable because he was committed to producing an album for Ike Turner."

xref.title: Industry Recognition and Collaborations
xref.body: Their talent garnered attention from prominent musicians; Jack White was such a fan that The White Stripes recorded one of their songs. They also developed friendships with members of Death Cab for Cutie and embarked on tours with acclaimed artists such as Neil Young, Weezer, The Black Keys, Cake, Bryan Adams, and Sious and Colour. "Jack White was such a fan that the white stripes recorded one of their songs. They became friends with members of Death Cab for Cutie."

xref.title: Influence on Dan Auerbach
xref.body: Junior Kimbrough, a blues singer, significantly influenced Dan Auerbach in high school. His music was a pivotal inspiration that led Auerbach to dedicate himself to playing the guitar full-time, ultimately leading to The Black Keys' tribute album, *Chulahoma*. "Dan was a big fan of this guy in high school. In fact, listening to Kimbrough, while smoking a lot of dope, helped him decide to pursue the guitar full time."

xref.title: Influence on The Black Keys' Growth
xref.body: The Black Keys' career benefited from the concurrent rise of The White Stripes, another prominent "garaji, punky, two-piece band." As The White Stripes gained more popularity, public interest in The Black Keys also grew, indicating a shared musical space and audience appreciation for their raw sound. "The bigger the white stripes got, the more interesting to grow in the black keys."

xref.title: New York Formation and Midwest Influences
xref.body: Singer Karen O. and drummer Brian Chase met at college in Ohio in the late 1990s. They later moved to New York, where they met photographer and guitarist Nick Zinner. Their initial band, Unitarred, evolved its sound to incorporate the "trashy, punky Garage Rock" Karen O. heard in Ohio, drawing influences from Detroit (140 miles up I-90) and Cleveland (35 miles east on Highway 10), near Akron (home of The Pretenders and The Black Keys). "Singer Karen O. met drummer Brian Chase at College in Ohio in the late 1990s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Revivals Part 4: Garage Rock

xref.title: Producer Collaboration with Black Keys
xref.body: Danger Mouse became The Black Keys' first external producer for their fifth album, *Attack and Release*, playing keyboards and bass on the record. He was initially unavailable due to a commitment to produce for Ike Turner, but that project's cancellation made him accessible. He later produced one song on *Brothers* and then fully produced and co-wrote all 11 tracks on *El Camino*. "Danger Mouse played a bunch of different instruments on the album, keyboards and bass mainly, and a few other musicians were called into filling with guitars and vocals and even clarinets."
